data.summary: Shared network folder as comms root is unsafe across PCs: naive-local timestamps break liveness, unlocked ensure_inbox truncate, unstealable remote locks, whole registry exposed
data.detail: Cross-PC investigation 2026-11-10 (sonnet accuracy-reviewed). now_timestamp() is datetime.now() naive local, so heartbeat_fresh/flap-kill/presence/id ordering mis-judge across time zones or >30s skew. ensure_inbox does unlocked exists() then open('w'), which a cached SMB not-found can turn into an inbox wipe; write_json_atomic has no retry on PermissionError. A lock held by a dead process on another host is never stolen (file_lock raises after 10s, file_lock_optional drops the write).
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: Investigation: cross-PC teammate-comms messaging — three proposals, relay-per-machine recommended (research only, no code)
data.detail: Colton asked (2026-11-10) how agents on separate PCs could message each other, suggesting an IP allowlist. Research only, peer-reviewed for accuracy by a sonnet subagent (17 claims: 11 confirmed, 6 partly, 0 wrong; 9 missed issues added). Proposals: (A) shared network folder via TEAMMATE_COMMS_DIR — zero code but unsafe as-is (see discovery on naive-local timestamps, ensure_inbox truncate, unstealable remote locks, SMB metadata caching; exposes the whole registry and tools like teammate_delete/compact requests to the other machine); consumer sync folders (OneDrive/Dropbox/Syncthing) are flatly unsupported. (B, recommended) each PC keeps its own local root; a standalone relay daemon per PC forwards messages to configured peers and calls the send core locally on the receiving side, so the recipient's existing watcher wakes it with no channel.py change; peers file = name + address + shared secret, HMAC-signed requests, store-and-forward spool, mirrored remote roster with liveness computed on the owning machine, message-only capability for remote peers. Addressing candidate name@machine (@ is outside AGENT_NAME_PATTERN) but _MENTION_RE in tools.py would false-match the machine part, so the mention parser must change. Groups need membership + transcript relay and deliver.py is DM-only, so groups are a later phase. (C) SSH + existing deliver CLI — one-way DM today with no new code, useful as a probe only. IP allowlist verdict: fine as a second layer and as the 'which machines' config, not sufficient alone on a plain LAN (DHCP churn, ARP spoofing, no user/process distinction); on a WireGuard mesh such as Tailscale the address is key-bound so an allowlist does identify the device. DESIGN.md's hard rule (real auth before any cross-host feature) applies. Platform claims were checked from reviewer knowledge, not live-tested on two machines. Open rulings for Colton: transport/network assumption, addressing form, whether groups are in the first release.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: Cross-machine relay first version built on wp/cross-machine-relay (uncommitted): plan + two sonnet reviews, relay.py, teammate_peers, 14-section test suite
data.detail: 2026-11-10, solo. Colton confirmed Tailscale stays required and asked for plan -> peer review -> first build -> peer review -> then a laptop test. Plan: docs/cross-machine-plan.md. Plan review (sonnet) found 5 blocking issues, all folded in before coding: private-group injection, message-id reuse defeating the author check, transient failures treated as poison, duplicate apply on crash, unbounded exchange size. Built: src/teammate_comms/relay.py (TailscaleNet from `tailscale status --json`, peers.json allowlist, per-peer outbox spool, single POST /v1/exchange endpoint on port 47821 carrying events both ways so only one machine needs inbound, seen-ring dedupe, roster sync with owner-computed liveness, status.json, comms-relay notices, detached autostart with a file_lock singleton); comms.py address helpers and remote-name guards on every inbox-path helper; tools.py remote branches in send_dm/send_group/react/delete_message/group handler, new post_group_record/deliver_dm_record/delete_group_local cores, mention regex, teammate_list remote section, teammate_profile name@machine, new teammate_peers tool; server.py reserves comms-relay and starts the relay on register. Implementation review (sonnet) found 4 must-fix, all fixed: uncapped retry on non-lock errors blocking a peer's queue, group members on unapproved machines getting a false 'queued', rejections of pulled events never reaching the sender, and the rejoin lockout (documented, not changed). Also fixed from it: posts never create groups, version restart only when the running relay is older, Tailscale status grace period, transient empty peers read no longer wipes state, reserved device names as machine names. Verified: tests/test_relay.py 14 sections pass; mutation checks reverted 12 protections and 11 were caught first time, the 12th after adding a three-machine assertion; five pre-existing suites pass; a real detached relay was started and stopped on Windows against the real (logged-out) Tailscale and reported tailscale_down. NOT verified: anything over a live tailnet, per-peer Tailscale fields on a real device, Windows Firewall behaviour, survival of the detached relay after the launching session exits. Deferred: remote read receipts, project profile sync, dashboard remote roster, late-joiner group history, team namespaces, id index for dedupe, sender notice on peer removal. The earlier ruling to retire avatars/compaction first was not a real dependency of this work and remains its own open task.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: Cross-machine group access is per machine: a peer may post/add to an existing local group only if its machine already has a member; groups are created only by membership events. Rejected: open cross-machine join
data.detail: Agent design decision forced by plan review (a peer guessing a private group's name could join it and receive its posts). Cost, accepted and documented: once a machine's last member leaves a group it cannot rejoin by itself; someone on a machine still in the group must add it. Enforced in relay.py _ensure_group/_machine_in_group.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: Relay exchange carries queued events in BOTH the request and the response, so two machines stay in sync when only one can accept inbound connections
data.detail: Each relay polls each peer with POST /v1/exchange; the response returns the responder's queue for the requester, acknowledged (or reported failed) on the requester's next request. At-least-once plus an id ring and an existing-message check gives once-only apply. This sidesteps Windows Firewall blocking inbound on one side, and failures must be reported in both directions (request `failed` list as well as response) or half the rejections go silent.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: Cross-machine relay v0.17.0 pushed: user-only peer approval + second peer review fixes
data.detail: Committed and pushed wp/cross-machine-relay (b5a4f12, then the review-fix commit). Peer approval moved out of the teammate_peers tool into the user command python -m teammate_comms.peers (owner ruling). A second independent sonnet review found no blockers and five should-fix items, all fixed: (1) a rejection whose response was lost was later answered as "applied" from the seen ring, so the author was never told — rejections are now stored with their reason in the seen file (id TAB reason) and replayed; (2) the printed approval command used a PowerShell-only "& " prefix when the python path has a space — now plain quoted form plus the PowerShell variant; (3) it now always includes --comms-dir; (4) group membership/delete, reaction and deletion events that could not be queued were silent — the author now gets a comms-relay DM; (5) per-request apply work is time-bounded (2 s) because each new message costs a transcript scan. Also: reactions/deletions only from a machine that is party to the target; ensure_relay returns failed if the child exits within 1 s, child stderr goes to relay.log. Mutation check: reverting fixes 1, 4 and the party check each fails the new tests (3 of 3). Not fixed, noted: future-dated ids from a skewed peer clock; remove_peer discards queued events silently; recovery-notice state lost on relay restart; id index. Still nothing verified over a live tailnet; laptop test planned next.

data.summary: First two-machine field test of the cross-machine relay (v0.17.0) passed: beepboop (desktop) and beepbooplegion (laptop) over Tailscale
data.detail: 2026-11-12. Loki pinned v0.17.0 at 8fca5e4 (marketplace commit d872e00, branch commit, main untouched). Local regression test on the installed plugin with Loki passed (DM, group, mention, reaction, group delete). Colton approved the laptop from this PC with the terminal command; the laptop approved back; state went to reachable with no firewall rule added. Verified across machines with a laptop session: DM both ways with wake; thumbsup/fire/100 reactions both ways with wake; group created with a remote member, mention flag, replies; deletion of a DM from each side shows a tombstone on the other; group deletion propagates; a remote member added to an existing local group (with a local-only member) works, and the local-only member sees the remote poster as name@machine. No comms-relay warnings, no errors. Findings: (1) teammate_peers reported NOT RUNNING for ~5 s after start because status.json was first written only after the first exchange attempt timed out — fixed by writing status before the peer loop. (2) Terminal-only peer approval was painful to set up; Colton reversed the 2026-11-10 ruling: teammate_peers gets add back (terminal command kept). (3) group join on a group missing locally raised a raw WinError 3 lock-path error — now a clear message. (4) The machines are in different timezones (UTC-6 vs UTC-7) and ~3 min apart in real time; message ids are naive local time, so ids from the two machines are an hour apart and id-based cursors/read positions are wrong across machines; Colton directed that message times be UTC, converted to local for display. (5) A remote member gets no notice when a shared group is deleted. (6) The detached relay survived the launching `!` command ending. Fixes 1-3 are in the working tree as v0.17.1, uncommitted.

data.summary: Colton ruled (2026-11-12): message ids move to UTC with each message carrying a send time shown in the reader's local time; ships bundled with the 0.17.1 fixes
data.detail: Chosen over (a) keeping local-time ids and adding a UTC field for display only, which leaves id-based read markers wrong across timezones, and (b) leaving as is. Heartbeats/presence stay local time because they never leave the machine and old/new sessions must agree on liveness. Accepted risk: sessions still on the old version write local-time ids that since-filters and unread badges can skip for up to the UTC offset, so all sessions on a machine restart when it updates. Bundling chosen over shipping 0.17.1 first: one update and restart instead of two.

data.summary: v0.17.1 built in the working tree: UTC message ids with a switchover floor and local-time send display, plus the field-test fixes; plan-reviewed and code-reviewed, uncommitted
data.detail: Built after the 2026-11-12 two-machine test. new_message_id(root) stamps UTC in the unchanged TIMESTAMP_FMT shape; heartbeats/presence/createdAt stay local via now_timestamp. Switchover floor: TeammateComms/id-floor.json holds the local wall-clock at the first UTC-era id (read as UTC) and the real epoch; stamp = max(utc_now, floor + max(0, now-created)/100). Message records carry ts (UTC epoch, ms); shown as "| sent: <local time>" in the inbox/history block and by the dashboard fmtWhen; relay passes ts only if plausible. Sonnet plan review found three blockers, all adopted: the original "UTC if >= floor else compressed" rule stepped backwards at hand-over (fixed with max); the floor only protects ids already on disk, not a still-running old-version session, which makes id cursors (since filters, reaction-wake cursor, dashboard cursors) skip between generations for up to the UTC offset, so docs now require restarting every session after updating; call-site list corrected (send_dm, group post, append_reaction, append_deletion x2). Sonnet code review found no must-fix; fixed: floor file now written whole to a temp file and hard-linked into place, corrupt file repaired by atomic replace, only a floor read back from the file is cached, floor file excluded from legacy_repopulated_entries, dashboard hourCycle h23, stale approval text. Also in 0.17.1: teammate_peers add restored, relay status written before the first exchange, clear error for joining a group missing locally. Mutation check: 8 of 8 reverted behaviours fail their tests (the status one after adding a test). All six suites pass. Not fixed, documented: DST fall-back hour at switchover; ids within 100 microseconds during the compressed window order by suffix; clock skew between machines still mis-orders views.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: Second two-machine test on v0.17.1 passed (UTC ids, local send time, peer remove/add via tool); v0.17.2 fix built for the stale-relay window
data.detail: 2026-11-12. v0.17.1 committed as 36e775a on wp/cross-machine-relay and pinned by Loki (marketplace commit 485aa78). Three-way group test (two desktop sessions, one laptop session): ids are UTC on both machines, sort in posting order, and every post shows "sent:" in the reader's own zone (-0600 desktop, -0700 laptop). Peer disconnect/reconnect with the tool alone worked from both machines: remove, a DM refused with "not an approved peer", a group post warning NOT SENT for the removed machine while still reaching the local member, add, reachable on the next status call. A post made while disconnected is not delivered later (by design). The laptop session refused to remove/add on a teammate's relayed permission and waited for its own user, which is the intended safeguard. Findings: (1) two posts received by the laptop before its session re-registered had no send time, because the laptop's relay process was still 0.17.0 and dropped the ts field; fixed in the working tree as v0.17.2 by calling ensure_relay from server start in a background thread. (2) While doing that, found ensure_relay stopped a running relay before checking TEAMMATE_RELAY_AUTOSTART=0; reordered so disabled autostart never stops one, and all test suites now set that variable so spawned test servers cannot touch a real relay. (3) The laptop's wall clock had been moved forward an hour with its timezone left on Mountain time, so its UTC is about an hour fast and its ids and send times are an hour in the future; a machine clock problem, not fixable in the product. (4) After a plugin update the client keeps the old tool list (teammate_peers still described without add) until a fresh session; the server accepts add regardless. (5) A relay with zero approved peers was still running when checked shortly after a remove. v0.17.2 is uncommitted.

data.summary: v0.17.3 built: MCP-surface audit fixes, teammate_readme tool, what-changed note and update-available notice ported from vibe-cognition; plan- and code-reviewed, uncommitted
data.detail: 2026-11-13, before handing the plugin to a coworker (Windows, Claude Code). Audit found only teammate_peers mentioned other machines, no guide for agents, the skill description still said "on one machine", nothing announced changes, and the 0.17.0 changelog entry described the reversed terminal-only approval. Built: name@machine wording in every tool description that takes a teammate name, teammate_peers with the four linking steps in order; teammate_readme (20th tool, no args, works unregistered, guide.py, names every tool); whats_new.py + .claude-plugin/whats-new.json and update_check.py ported from vibe-cognition; harness.py gained manifest paths, URL templates and env names so the new modules carry no harness literals; hooks/session-start.sh runs both modules after the venv step, each printing one JSON-escaped ASCII line, joined with the first-build message into additionalContext; tests/test_notices.py plus a CI step; relay CI step made independent of the Codex suite, which has failed on Windows/macOS on main since September. Sonnet plan review found five blockers, all adopted: server instructions would have reversed WP-41 (owner then ruled no usage instructions pushed, only what changed and update available); the literal ratchet in test_codex; multi-line notes breaking the hook JSON; the consistency test missing from CI; the first-build exit skipping the notes on every update. Deviations from vibe-cognition, deliberate: a machine with no marker gets the recent entries once (owner wants a first install to say what changed); both notices are skipped under Codex (2000-char context budget, its marketplace does not list the plugin). Sonnet code review found no must-fix; fixed: "do not resend" scoped to queued messages (NOT SENT / NOT QUEUED need a resend), guide gained the missing warning states and the registration and team-namespace requirements, what-changed bullets no longer name tools, remote version and commit id strictly validated with a response size cap, stale plugin descriptions, changelog prerequisites. Mutation check 10 of 10. All seven suites pass; test_relay's connection-authorization section timed out once and passed on re-runs (suspected load flake). Live update check against the real marketplace worked. Owner also ruled Mac/Linux need not be supported for now.

data.summary: 0.17.3 field test (sleep/queue test passed, what-changed note lost) and v0.17.4 build: note shown until confirmed
data.detail:
2026-11-16. Desktop beepboop and laptop beepbooplegion on 0.17.3 (pinned at 21e22f6).

Sleep test PASSED. Laptop entered sleep 14:48:45 local; a DM sent 34 s later queued with a WARNING. For the first minute the warning said "online in Tailscale but nothing answers on port 47821" and printed the firewall command, because Tailscale had not yet marked the device offline; after 60 s comms-relay sent NOT DELIVERED with the correct reason (offline: powered off, asleep or disconnected). Laptop woke 15:36:18; the message arrived about 5 s later after 47 minutes, the recipient was woken by the channel notice with no user prompt, the sent: time was the original send time, and comms-relay told the sender the machine was reachable again. Gaps noted, not fixed: misleading firewall reason in the first minute after sleep; the relay log has no line for sleep, resume or delivery.

Stale time zone: a relay/server process started before a Windows time zone change keeps the old zone (sent: showed -0700 instead of -0600; relay.log lines an hour apart across a restart). A restart fixes it. Not a rendering bug.

Relay replacement confirmed on a real update: the laptop's 0.17.2 relay was stopped and 0.17.3 started before the session registered.

What-changed note LOST on both machines. Desktop: the session-start hook (SessionStart:resume, after /plugin update, /reload-plugins, failed /mcp) ran once per the transcript, wrote the venv stamp, whats-new-seen and update-check.json, and its recorded stdout held only the "built its environment for the first time" line. Laptop: the hook ran (same three files written) but the transcript has no hook_success record at all and nothing reached the model. No other session on the desktop was active at that second. Could not reproduce: five runs delivered the note (hand runs on normal and first-build paths, bare venv created first by uv run --no-sync, and three headless claude -p sessions including --plugin-dir with no venv). Best-fitting explanation, unproven: on resume after an in-session update the harness runs the hook in a pass whose output is discarded, and on the desktop two near-simultaneous runs raced (old code wrote the marker before comparing, so the second run saw seen == installed and printed nothing).

Fix built as v0.17.4 (uncommitted at time of recording): whats_new.plan() returns (note, commit); printing only counts a showing in whats-new-pending.json; the marker advances on teammate_readme(changes_seen=true) (whats_new.confirm, strict JSON true, refuses when the manifest at the server's plugin root differs from the running version), on the 5th unconfirmed showing, or when there is nothing to show. Unique temp file per atomic write. Hook keeps a module's output even if it exits non-zero. Pre-build sonnet review: three blockers adopted (literal ratchet, stale server, shared temp name); docs confirmed MCP stdio servers get CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT and CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA in their environment, so no env block was added. Post-build sonnet review: no blockers; added a test pinning the cap at 5 (the only mutation not caught). Known residual: a server left running from the previous version confirms only its own version, so the new note keeps showing until a reconnected server confirms or the cap is reached. All four suites pass (notices, handshake, codex, relay). The confirm call has not yet been exercised in a live session.

data.summary: v0.17.4 live verification on both machines: what-changed note, confirm call and three-way messaging all pass
data.detail: On 2026-11-17 after the marketplace pin (87b16dc -> teammate-comms 70dd7fd), Colton updated the plugin in all three sessions (two on desktop beepboop, one on laptop beepbooplegion) by in-session update, reload and MCP reconnect, the same sequence that lost the note on 0.17.3. This time the what-changed note (v0.17.3 -> v0.17.4) reached all three sessions as session-start hook context; each told Colton and called teammate_readme(changes_seen=true), which returned "Recorded: the what-changed note for v0.17.4 will not be shown again". On the desktop the seen marker reads 0.17.4 and whats-new-pending.json is gone. Both relays were replaced by 0.17.4 before registration (desktop relay.log: stop requested, relay 0.17.4 starting pid 110272). Messaging: desktop-to-laptop direct message delivered in about 2 seconds with correct send time and a wake; laptop-to-desktop reply woke the desktop session; a group post with mentions reached the second desktop session and the laptop session, and both group replies came back; a direct message from the second desktop session to the laptop carried no warning. data.detail: Seen on the laptop on 0.17.4: the warning named pid 23356, which no longer existed; it was the same session's previous server from before the reconnect. The desktop did not show it in the same sequence, so it depends on timing. Checking that the named pid is still alive on the same host before warning would remove the false alarm. Not fixed.

data.summary: Colton ruled (2026-11-17): cross-machine comms are for one person's own machines on one tailnet; cross-tailnet or cross-company messaging is out of scope
data.detail: The relay is meant to link the same user's machines, which are assumed to be on the same Tailscale tailnet. A coworker who gets the plugin uses it among their own machines on their own tailnet. Shared-device or cross-tailnet setups do not need to be supported or tested; this closes the open question about the coworker's Tailscale relationship.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: Colton ruled (2026-11-17): teammate_reincarnate must work across peers; the receiving machine obeys only after a per-peer opt-in stored with the peers list, off by default
data.detail: Reverses the 2026-11-10 ruling that cross-machine spawning was out (node 88e90ada2127). Rejected: letting any added peer spawn with no extra step (adding a peer for messaging would silently grant agent-launching power), and reusing TEAMMATE_REINCARNATE_ENABLED on the receiver (the relay inherits its environment from whichever session started it, so it would vary between restarts and cannot tell peers apart).
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: Colton ruled (2026-11-17): the remote-spawn opt-in is one switch per machine (accept spawns from any approved peer), not a per-peer permission
data.detail: Refines the earlier ruling the same day (node 31a35e67fe14), which stored the opt-in per named peer. Reason given: the user already manages their Tailscale network and approved-peer list, so naming peers again adds friction without adding control. The switch stays off by default and is set on the receiving machine.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: Colton ruled (2026-11-17): add a teammate shutdown tool that works locally and across peers; closes the session immediately; any registered teammate may use it; remote use is covered by the same per-machine switch as spawning
data.detail: Purpose: manage agents on all of the user's machines from one machine. Rejected for closing style: warn-wait-close (a busy agent sees the warning too late, slower, more to maintain) and a caller-chosen wait. Rejected for authority: manager-only (most agents have no manager set) and requiring the switch on the same machine (would force opening the machine to peers just to use it locally). A closed session keeps its history and can be resumed.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: Windows Terminal splits wt.exe arguments on an unescaped semicolon, cutting a spawn prompt at its first ";"; escaping as "\;" passes it through intact
data.detail: Confirmed by experiment on 2026-11-17: wt.exe -d dir -- python show.py "one; two; three" delivered only "one"; with "one\; two\; three" the child received the whole string. This affected local spawn since 0.6.0. spawn_in_terminal now escapes every wt argument.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: Ending a session's harness process with exit code 0 makes Windows Terminal close its tab by itself; exit code 1 leaves a dead tab. No extra process needs closing
data.detail: Verified live on 2026-11-17 with a real throwaway session: TerminateProcess(harness, 1) left the tab's console host running, TerminateProcess(harness, 0) removed it. Only applies when the harness is the tab's own program (a spawned session); a session started inside a shell leaves the shell. Depends on the profile's close-on-exit setting not being "never". Downside: a forced close looks like a normal quit to anything chained on the exit code.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: The per-machine relay is a child process of whichever session's server started it, so killing a session's process tree by parent pid also kills the relay unless it is explicitly protected
data.detail: Found by the implementation peer review of teammate_shutdown and confirmed against the live desktop: the relay's parent pid resolved to a running session. ensure_relay detaches the relay from the console and job but the parent pid remains. close_session now takes a protect set and close_own_session passes the relay pid from status.json; a protected pid and everything below it are skipped.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: Cross-machine control requests (spawn, shutdown) are refused when the peer is unreachable and dropped by the sender after 45 s, never queued; outcome is reported from the sender's own applied/rejected acknowledgements, with no reply event
data.detail: Messages queue for an offline machine, but an action that starts or closes a process must never fire late. The sending relay ages control events by its own clock, so no cross-machine clock comparison is needed. Reporting from _settle avoids a reply event that a peer could use to inject text as comms-relay. On the receiver, a per-name cooldown is persisted before the launch so a crash-and-resend cannot launch twice.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: v0.18.0 built (uncommitted): teammate_spawn and new teammate_shutdown work across peers behind a per-machine remote control switch
data.detail: On 2026-11-17 Colton asked for reincarnate to work across peers, then for a cross-peer shutdown tool, a rename of teammate_reincarnate to teammate_spawn, and for the shutdown to clean up its terminal tab if that could be done safely. Plan was peer reviewed twice (spawn, then shutdown) before building and the implementation once after. Built: remote spawn and shutdown as relay event kinds; a per-machine switch (accept_remote_control / refuse_remote_control in teammate_peers and the peers terminal command, relay/settings.json, fail closed) with a roster hint so senders refuse early; control requests refused when the peer is unreachable and dropped after 45 s; receiver rate limit and persisted per-name cooldown; child environment scrubbed and pinned to the relay's comms root; shutdown carried out by the target's own server through a request file bound to its instance id, using new procs.py (ctypes Toolhelp) to find the harness among its ancestors and end that process tree. Plan review changes adopted: no reply event (outcome reported from the sender's own acknowledgements), receiver default harness, fail-closed settings file, in-process termination instead of taskkill, refuse rather than guess when the harness cannot be identified (native installs only). Implementation review found that shutdown would kill the machine's relay when the target session had started it (now protected), that a failed close looked like success (now nothing is touched and the requester is told), a misleading queued notice for control requests, a case-sensitive cooldown, and eight untested guards; all fixed, and 15 mutation checks are caught. Verified live on the desktop: a real throwaway session on the dev server was shut down in about 0.55 s with its record marked offline and its tab closed; a windowless detached process can open a terminal; the semicolon escape works. Not yet verified: any real cross-machine spawn or shutdown, which needs 0.18.0 on both machines. All seven test suites pass. Awaiting Colton's go-ahead to commit, push and pin.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.reason: 2026-11-17 ruling reverses the 2026-11-10 exclusion of cross-machine teammate spawning
Per-machine switch replaces the per-peer opt-in for remote spawn
Remote shutdown is governed by the same per-machine switch defined in the other ruling

data.summary: A spawned Claude Code session in a never-opened folder stops at the workspace trust question and never registers; nothing else is started until a person answers
data.detail: Seen live on the desktop 2026-11-17 (Claude Code 2.1.327) in a temp folder. Trust is recorded in .claude.json under projects[folder].hasTrustDialogAccepted (forward-slash keys); a parent counts up to the repository root, the home folder never does. MCP servers do not start before the answer, so the session cannot report its own stall.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: Remote spawn refuses a folder the harness has not trusted and reports a launch that has not registered after 90 s; trust is only read, never granted by the plugin
data.detail: Chosen: read-only check of Claude Code's trust record before launching (unknown means launch) plus an in-memory watchdog in the receiving relay that messages the requester once. Rejected: writing hasTrustDialogAccepted for the user, because it would let another machine waive a safety question and would edit a file Claude Code itself rewrites. Local spawn only warns, since a person is at that machine.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: Mutation check opened a real Claude terminal on the desktop: a spawn test ran outside the fake launcher, so removing the guard it tested launched for real
data.detail: tests/test_relay.py called apply_event with a spawn from an unapproved machine without the Launches stub; with the approved-peer guard mutated away the real launcher ran in a temp folder. Fixed by wrapping that check in Launches and asserting nothing launched. Any test that can reach spawn_in_terminal must run under the stub.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.reason: Discovery that a spawned session in an untrusted folder stalls at the trust dialog led to the decision to check trust before remote launch and add a registration watchdog.

data.summary: 0.18.0 hardening pass: trust check, outcome watches, three reviews and a fresh-agent surface audit
data.detail: After the 0.18.0 remote spawn and shutdown build, a spawned session was seen stalled at Claude Code's folder trust question. Added a read-only trust check on the receiver (harness.folder_trusted) and a watch that reports a launch that never came online. Then ran a double check, an adversarial sonnet review, a fresh-agent audit of the tool surface, and a verification review of the fixes. Fixes from the reviews: control events now carry their age by the sender's clock and the receiver rejects a missing or over-45-second age; the sender's expiry sweep runs every tick so an unreachable peer no longer delays the drop; a request stamped ahead of the clock counts as expired; the NOT CONFIRMED text says the request may already have been carried out; launch and shutdown watches moved from memory to relay/awaiting.json (survives a relay restart, checked every 5 s, liveness read outside the relay lock) and a shutdown still running after 20 s is reported; procs.terminate checks creation time on the same handle it ends, so a reused pid is never ended; close_session reports the session closed only if the session pid itself ended; check_shutdown_target refuses a record with no instance_id; local shutdown reports closed only when the target server pid is gone; spawn cooldown blocks a future-stamped launch; a prompt cannot start with a dash; the stall report is queued directly instead of through send_dm so the relay never calls ensure_relay on itself; trust never reaches up through the home folder. Surface: the guide gained a full Remote control section with preconditions and every outcome message, defines comms-relay as a system sender, says a busy teammate cannot be interrupted, and no longer claims spawning on another machine is impossible. Tests: relay tests can no longer open a real terminal (module-level stub records a failure), 19 new mutation checks all caught against a passing baseline, seven suites pass. Commits 96f8625, 7be0456, 0f5b36d, 1f5330a on wp/cross-machine-relay, pushed, not pinned. Not done: no real two-machine spawn or shutdown yet; design points left as ruled (any agent can turn the switch on, local shutdown is ungated); description bloat (legacy avatar and compaction tools, duplicated profile fields) reported but not trimmed.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: Cross-machine time limits: send the request's age by the sender's clock and let the receiver reject on age; never compare two machines' clocks
data.detail: Sender-only expiry left a window where a request built just inside the limit was applied after it. Stamping age at batch time and rejecting missing or excessive age on arrival bounds lateness to network time, and treating a future-stamped request as expired covers a clock that stepped back.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.reason: Sender-only expiry in the earlier pattern left a late-apply window; the review finding led to the receiver-side age check.
Test-opened-real-terminal fail fixed by the hardening episode's module-level launcher stub that records a failure.

data.summary: Grok Bot (xAI cloud agent) can be a teammate via webhook doorbell + hosted MCP mailbox: field-tested 2026-11-18, both directions, 64 KB intact, unattended
data.detail: Live test with a real Grok Bot account. Routine webhook (POST, Bearer key, JSON body) starts a run but is unfit to carry content: a top-level field named "context" is silently stripped, bodies between about 2 KB and 8 KB get truncated before the run sees them, the response is only a runUuid, each run starts with no memory, and the bot's own reports contradict each other. A throwaway Cloudflare Worker (Durable Object, hand-rolled JSON-only MCP over POST, separate bot and PC bearer keys) worked as a mailbox: the bot connected through an mcp-remote proxy on its cloud computer reading the key from a masked env secret, identified as "Cursor (via mcp-remote)", fetched and replied with no approval prompt, and a webhook-triggered routine run handled a 63,883-character message exactly. No official API exists to read a bot's output; unofficial grok-bot-mcp project rejected (internal Cursor endpoints).
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.reason: Both concern bringing a non-Claude harness into teammate-comms as a teammate; Codex parity plan is the precedent for harness-neutral teammates.

data.summary: Cloud agents (Grok Bot) join via a user-deployed mailbox Worker as a virtual machine name with direct messages only; linking is terminal-only, never an agent tool action
data.detail: Chosen with Colton away, on his standing preference for the lowest-risk option. Rejected: carrying content in the Grok webhook (drops a field named context, truncates past about 2 KB), the unofficial grok-bot-mcp project (internal Cursor endpoints), a public door on the PC, and exposing link_mailbox to agents (peer review proved a prompt-injected agent could link or repoint a mailbox and capture mail). read_peers stays real peers only; read_mailboxes/read_links are separate so unmoved call sites refuse a mailbox by default. Open for Colton: recipient allow list per link, default daily doorbell limit.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: v0.19.0: cloud mailbox so a Grok Bot can exchange direct messages with local agents
data.detail: Colton asked whether teammate-comms could work with Grok Bot. Research of xAI docs plus hands-on tests on his account showed: routine webhooks start a run but cannot carry content; a custom MCP server by address works with the key in a masked env secret (the bot used an mcp-remote proxy); a webhook-started run fetched and replied through a throwaway Worker with no approval prompt, 63,883 characters exact. Plan written (docs/cloud-mailbox-plan.md) and peer reviewed before build; the review moved inbound mail off the peer event path, added purpose-explicit address resolution, a separate sync thread, deferral instead of rejection for a full mailbox, a banner on cloud messages and a daily doorbell cap. Built: mailbox-worker (dependency-free Worker, one Durable Object, node --test with a Map-backed store, make_config.py key generator), src/teammate_comms/mailbox.py, relay and tools integration, README walkthrough, guide, DESIGN section 17. Code peer review then proved a confused-deputy hole in the agent-facing link action, header forgery through reply_to, mailbox-controlled text reaching an urgent comms-relay notice, Object-inherited names matching in the Worker, head-of-line blocking by deferred mail, a doorbell that went silent forever, and NaN last_seen breaking the list; all fixed, with linking made terminal-only and keys prefixed tcm_/tcb_. Verification: 8 Python suites and 21 Worker tests pass; the real relay code ran against the real Worker under wrangler dev (19 checks incl. a full-size 4-byte-character message and the alarm-driven doorbell); 39 of 40 mutations caught, the survivor being an equivalent mutant. Not done: a real Grok Bot against the new Worker (needs Colton to deploy it, repoint the bot and paste the doorbell); the spike Worker teammate-grok-mailbox-spike is still deployed on his account.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: An action that sends a local secret or opens a channel to a caller-chosen address must not be an agent tool action: make it a terminal command the user runs, and have the tool print it
data.detail: Format rules on the secret file and the URL shrink the hole but do not close it, because a prompt-injected agent can write its own well-formed file and choose its own server. Keep the safe direction (unlink, list) in the tool. Also treat every string a remote service returns as untrusted text: force one clipped line and attribute it before an agent sees it.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.reason: The Grok Bot field test showed the webhook strips a context field and truncates bodies over about 2 KB and that a hosted MCP mailbox works; these findings are the stated basis for the mailbox Worker decision.

data.summary: deliver_dm_record ran a recipient liveness probe (tasklist subprocess, ~0.6 s on Windows) on every relayed message although the relay ignores the result; now skipped with report_live=False
data.detail: Found by profiling when a 5-second apply budget let only 7 cloud messages through per pass. It affected messages from peer machines too, applied under the relay lock: 50 inbound messages took about 35 s and could make status go stale. After the change 50 deliver in under 2 s.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: v0.19.1: Worker renamed cloud-mailbox-worker, example mailbox cloudbot, final review and fresh-agent surface audit fixes
data.detail: Colton asked for the Worker to be renamed cloud-mailbox-worker with agents reading CommsTest@cloudbot, so the feature is not tied to Grok, then for a last peer review and a surface audit. Rename: folder, deployed Worker name, docs and tests; version 0.19.1. Surface audit (three audiences: local agent, cloud bot, human following the README) found a naive local agent could not discover cloud agents and was steered to add a peer; the cloud bot was not told to check mail first, stop when empty, how to reply, or that comms-relay is a system sender; README commands failed on Windows (tilde, python, no plugin folder). Fixed in tool descriptions, error texts, guide, Worker instructions, README; re-read mail is now marked answered when a reply_to was sent; the printed link command carries --comms-dir. Final code review confirmed terminal-only linking, key-file rule, hasOwn and doorbell fixes hold, and found: inbound cap defeated by rotating sender names and unbounded tracking; apply under the relay lock with no budget; one bot starving others via the shared 500 queue; header neutralising missed mid-line and odd line breaks; unattributed mailbox text in several places; unbounded bot names; make_config accepting a hostless doorbell. All fixed: over-limit mail is refused back, per-mailbox cap 180, per-bot 200 uncollected in the Worker, apply outside the lock with a 5 s budget, neutralise anywhere, said() attribution, held mail skipped by file name. Verification: 8 Python suites, 21 Worker tests, real-Worker run under wrangler dev, 15 of 15 mutations caught (1 skipped on a bad anchor). Not pinned at the time of writing; real Grok Bot against the new Worker still untested.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.reason: Profiling discovery of a slow per-message liveness probe on the relay apply path; the v0.19.1 episode reworked that same apply path (apply outside the lock with a 5 s budget).

data.summary: Mailbox identity is per account, not per bot: one token per shared connector, named bots under it, each call passes its own name (me); bots in one account are one trust unit
data.detail: Field use showed Grok Bot and Rakazo both share a connector and its secret across every agent in an account or space, so a second bot used the first one's connector and took its mail. Rejected: one connector per bot (not possible in Rakazo, by convention only in Grok), bots self-registering names or doorbells (a self-chosen webhook address is an abuse path), a name check as mere guard. Names and doorbells stay in the user's config; me selects the inbox and is not authentication. Supersedes the one-key-per-bot rule in the 0.19.0 design.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: v0.19.2: accounts for shared connectors, full-mailbox rejection, long names shortened, DPAPI key storage; first Rakazo field test
data.detail: Colton ruled the three known gaps must be fixed: a full mailbox rejects to the sender with a reason (limits raised to 5,000 per bot and per machine, 2,000 per bot per machine; hold-and-retry and the mailbox_full state deleted); an agent name over 64 characters is shortened for the mailbox and a reply mapped back, refused when it stands for more than one agent session; the machine key is sealed with Windows DPAPI via ctypes (option A; a Worker secret cannot hold it because the machine needs its own copy readable unattended). A Grok chat showed connectors and secrets are shared by all bots in an account; research (xAI docs) confirmed it and compared Rakazo (open source, self-hostable, per-space connectors in practice, bearer MCP, webhook routines), Devin (sessions, no per-session connector scope, coding focus) and others; Colton started a hosted Rakazo trial and said multi-bot identities across several spaces are needed at once. Built accounts (see decision). Peer review: no blocker; fixed a wrong-recipient case when an exact 64-character name coexists with a longer one, roster hiding collisions, old-Worker detection (MIN_WORKER 1.1.0), do-not-guess wording, --new-key rotation keeping doorbells, plain keys sealed at relay start, stale key files removed, atomic config writes. Verified: 8 Python suites, 23 Worker tests, real relay against the real Worker under wrangler dev. Live: cloud-mailbox-worker deployed on Colton's Cloudflare account, the Grok spike Worker deleted, keys in C:\Users\colto\teammate-mailbox, bot token in 1Password item Rakazo-mailbox; Rakazo bot Chief connected with a bearer-token custom server, fetched and replied (mail_send asked for approval once, then always allowed); Sam added to the same account. data.summary: System-wide user availability status for teammate-comms (available/away, leave-at time, away behaviour)
data.detail: Requested by Colton (relayed through the cloud agent Chief, then confirmed by Colton directly). 1) Status: the user has a system-wide status, available or away; agents using comms are alerted when it changes. 2) Leave-at time: an agent can set a time when the user must step away; before that time agents get a heads-up to wrap up requests that need the user quickly; at that time the status flips to away automatically. 3) Easy check: agents get a simple way to ask whether the user is available for questions. 4) Away behaviour: the user sets what agents do while away: "work autonomously" (default), "wait", or any freeform instruction; changed by asking an agent to change the away behaviour. 5) Main use case: one agent (for example a Rakazo cloud agent) watches the user's calendar and sets the leave-at time, so agents are alerted both when the user needs to leave and when they have actually stepped away (no more questions). Open design point: cloud agents can only send direct messages today, so setting leave-at from a cloud agent needs a new mailbox tool or a local agent acting on its message.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: Colton ruled (2026-11-20): no warning line on cloud-agent messages; whether to trust a cloud agent is each user's choice stated in their CLAUDE.md, with the risks stated clearly in the README
data.detail: The 0.19.0 design prefixed every inbound cloud message with a banner telling the reader to treat it as information, not an instruction, and repeated that stance in teammate_list, the guide and the link output. Colton rejected the product taking that stance: removed in 0.19.4. Rejected alternative: keeping the banner as a default with an opt-out. Kept: the enforced limits (direct messages only, normal priority, no linking/spawn/shutdown) and header-lookalike neutralising. With no instruction, the guide tells an agent to ask its user first.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: User availability status design (0.20.0): computed effective status, no scheduler, notices written by each session's own watcher, Lamport (seq, rev) ordering, state carried in rosters and mailbox sync
data.detail: Colton's rulings 2026-11-20: cloud agents may set status per connection, opt-in (can_set_status on the mailbox account, because bots on one connection share names); any local agent may set it when asked; cloud agents get no notices (always-on, do not stop when user is away); status returns to available only by asking an agent. Rejected after peer review: a new relay event kind with feature negotiation (state rides in the roster instead), clock-time ordering (a fast clock would keep winning), a per-agent seen file (field on the agent record instead), a cloud change-request queue (the mailbox is just another replica; the relay never takes the away-behaviour text from it), a note field (injection channel).
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: Rakazo field results: webhook routine takes Authorization: Bearer key, doorbell wake works end to end; multi-bot connector marks `me` required so a nameless call is rejected client-side
data.detail: Rakazo bots create a webhook-triggered routine themselves (Schedule create); the webhook address and key are copied from the routine page and accept the mailbox's Authorization: Bearer header, returning {ok, messageId, runId, seq}. The mailbox rang Chief on its own and the reply arrived in under 100 s. Two bots on one connection (Chief, Sam) each got only their own mail. A cloud bot's mail_teammates shows every registered full agent on the machine across all projects (31 here). Reply timestamps showed the PC clock about 3 s ahead of Cloudflare.

Field tests on the real relay and Worker with Rakazo bots Chief and Sam: link via terminal command worked, real teammate_send both ways, refusal for an unknown cloud name came back in half a second, two bots on one connection stayed separate, a nameless call was refused, Chief's webhook doorbell (Authorization: Bearer) was configured in the mailbox config and woke Chief unaided. 0.19.4 (372897a): Colton had the cloud-message warning banner removed; trust in a cloud agent is the user's choice in their standing instructions, README gained a risks section; peer review found leftover stance text in README/DESIGN and a leading-whitespace reply-line lookalike, fixed by stripping leading blank space. 0.20.0 (96c20ee): user availability status from backlog task 95f3b2135776, relayed by Chief and confirmed by Colton. Plan (docs/availability-plan.md) was peer reviewed before building, which replaced clock ordering with a (seq, rev) counter, a new event kind with roster carry, a seen file with a record field, and a cloud request queue with treating the mailbox as a replica. Built availability.py, tool teammate_user_status, watcher-delivered notices from comms-status, roster and mailbox carry, Worker 1.2.0 tools user_status and user_set_status gated per account by can_set_status. data.summary: Cloud mailbox arc (v0.19.0 to v0.20.0): cloud agents join as direct-message teammates through a user-deployed Worker
data.detail: Began 2026-11-18 with a Grok Bot field test: a routine webhook could not carry content (context field stripped, bodies over about 2 KB truncated), so a hosted MCP mailbox was built; the bot handled a 63,883-character message exactly. v0.19.0 shipped the cloud-mailbox Worker and mailbox module; its decision (direct messages only, terminal-only linking) was later superseded by the per-account identity decision, because a shared connector let a second bot take the first bot's mail. The terminal-only linking pattern generalizes: actions sending a local secret or opening a channel to a caller-chosen address must be terminal commands. v0.19.1 renamed the Worker to cloud-mailbox-worker and fixed surface-audit gaps; v0.19.2 fixed full-mailbox rejection, limits, long names and DPAPI key sealing, with the first Rakazo field test. A profiling discovery found a per-message liveness probe on the relay apply path. Rakazo field results confirmed the bearer-token doorbell and that multi-bot connectors need an explicit name per call. v0.19.3 to v0.20.0 (summarized separately) removed the warning banner and added user availability status. This is the umbrella for the whole arc.
data.author: Colton Dyck

data.summary: Availability: a request matching the current state is a no-op and re-alerts nobody (Colton, 2026-11-20)
data.detail: Colton ruled that if the user is already away and an agent sets the status again by accident, agents must not be alerted again. Implemented in availability.change and the Worker's userSetStatus: away while effectively away (explicit or via a passed leave time), available while available with no pending leave time, and an identical leave time, heads-up or away behaviour leave seq/rev/behaviour_rev untouched, so watchers see no new snapshot. The tool answers "Nothing changed..."; the Worker answers recorded:false. Side effect: marking away after a leave time has passed no longer converts the state to an explicit away; away_since still derives from the leave time. Rejected: suppressing only the notice while still bumping the counter (would still churn every replica and rename the setter).
context: unreleased; follows decision on user availability status design

data.summary: Why the MCP server failed in the first session after every plugin update: bare venv from `uv run --no-sync`, fixed by launch.py (0.20.1)
data.detail: Each update installs into a new versioned cache folder with no .venv. Claude Code spawns the MCP server before the SessionStart hook's uv sync finishes; `uv run --no-sync` then creates a bare venv with nothing installed, so `python -m teammate_comms.server` dies with ModuleNotFoundError and the harness caches the failure for 15 min. Fix: plugin.json now runs ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/launch.py, which puts <root>/src on sys.path and calls server.main(), needing no install. Rejected: PYTHONPATH in the plugin env block (spawned sessions and the relay's restored PYTHONPATH would inherit it). Verified on six fresh copies with uv sync racing the start. Codex adapter left unchanged: it registers the server after its own sync and its venv lives in the data dir. Sonnet review found nothing important. Kept minor risk: the broker's plugin-runtime.json python cannot `-m teammate_comms.deliver` until the hook's sync completes (seconds).
data.author: Colton Dyck
